claims.text: The multielement mixture in HEAs promotes preferential elemental partitioning during high-temperature oxidation.
Preferential elemental partitioning leads to a continuous, adherent, and slow-growing oxide layer.
The protective oxide scale is enriched in oxidation-resistant elements such as chromium or aluminum.
High mixing entropy enhances the beneficial segregation of chromium or aluminum.
The enriched oxide scale reduces oxygen and metal-cation diffusion relative to conventional alloys.
A continuous, adherent Cr- or Al-enriched oxide scale acts as a barrier to oxygen ingress and metal-ion diffusion.
During high-temperature oxidation, the multicomponent nature of an HEA drives selected elements to segregate to the surface.
The surface-segregated elements form a protective oxide.
High mixing entropy reduces chemical-potential gradients.
Reduced chemical-potential gradients slow the diffusion of oxygen and alloy cations.
Slower oxygen and cation diffusion produces a more stable and slowly growing oxide layer.
Relative to the conventional-alloy baseline, the HEA will form a thicker and more uniform protective oxide scale.
Relative to the conventional-alloy baseline, the HEA oxide scale will grow more slowly.
The HEA will show less oxidation-associated weight gain over time than the conventional alloy.
The HEA oxide scale will adhere better than the oxide scale on the conventional alloy.
The proposed mechanism applies under high-temperature oxidation in oxygen-rich environments.
The mechanism may not extend to lower temperatures or non-oxidizing atmospheres because oxidation kinetics and elemental partitioning differ.
